metadata.title: Strong Performers and Successful Reformers in Education: Lessons from PISA for Mexico

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report synthesizes PISA results across multiple cycles (reading 2000/2009, mathematics 2003/2009, science 2006/2009) and compares Mexico to OECD, G20, and GDP-similar benchmark groups. The report discusses weighting at the school level: principals’ questionnaire responses are weighted to be proportional to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in each school when school-level characteristics are presented. For student-level achievement comparisons, the report points readers to the PISA 2009 technical documentation for the underlying PISA scaling and estimation procedures; it does not provide explicit student weight variable names in the excerpt. Because this is a descriptive benchmarking and policy lessons report (not an original student-level ML analysis), the appropriate “weights” are those embedded in the official PISA estimation outputs rather than weights applied by the authors in a new model.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not directly handled in this report because it does not fit predictive models on PV-based achievement outcomes; instead, it reports descriptive statistics (mean scores, proficiency shares, and differences) and policy interpretations using published PISA results. Missing-data handling is therefore not specified as an analytic step in this report’s own methodology; the report instead refers readers to the PISA technical documentation and uses PISA’s published indicators. This is a reporting/secondary-analysis context rather than an original microdata estimation study.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses PISA target population definitions (15-year-olds aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months, at least 6 years of formal schooling) and focuses on Mexico’s performance trends across PISA cycles: reading (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009), mathematics (2003, 2006, 2009), and science (2006, 2009). For cross-country trend comparisons, it restricts to countries with valid results for the relevant pairs of years (e.g., 38 countries with valid reading results in 2000 and 2009; 39 for mathematics in 2003 and 2009; 56 for science in 2006 and 2009). For benchmarking tables, it uses PISA 2009 results for 15-year-olds and reports that some partner economies conducted PISA in 2010 instead of 2009. The report does not specify additional microdata inclusion/exclusion rules beyond reliance on PISA’s published databases and the PISA reporting symbols for missing/withdrawn data.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report is a descriptive benchmarking and policy lessons synthesis using PISA results for Mexico across multiple cycles (reading from 2000 onward, mathematics from 2003, and science from 2006). It reports Mexico’s mean country scores and proficiency distributions, including whether changes are statistically significant, and compares Mexico to OECD averages and to selected benchmark groups (OECD, G20, and countries with similar GDP per capita). The report also examines equity by relating performance to students’ socio-economic background using the PISA ESCS index and highlights changes in the strength of that association over time. For internal benchmarking, it uses school-level aggregates (school ESCS profiles and school performance) to show that performance varies substantially even among schools serving students with similar socio-economic backgrounds. The report does not conduct new student-level ML modeling; instead, it interprets published PISA estimates and links them to reform priorities for Mexico.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a secondary OECD policy report that summarizes published PISA results rather than an original empirical study that fits predictive models. As a result, fields that would normally be populated for an ML paper (e.g., PV handling in the authors’ own estimation, missing-data imputation strategy, ML algorithms, and model performance metrics) are not applicable in the sense of being part of the report’s own analytic pipeline. The report does provide methodological context (PISA target population, reporting symbols for missing data, and references to PISA technical documentation), but it does not specify an author-run estimation procedure with explicit weights, PV combination rules, or missing-data handling steps.
